title: I Worked at LinkedIn. Here’s How to Fix Your Profile.
summary: Part one of the hosts' LinkedIn Masterclass, drawing on Cherie's nearly five years at LinkedIn (profile team and LinkedIn Learning) and the class she teaches at Stanford GSB on writing a winning About section. They explain why a filled-out profile makes you discoverable (it is all metadata), present the 'three S's' framework (share, sell, search-optimized), walk through beginner, intermediate and advanced real-profile examples, and close with the test of whether you can name the one sentence you want readers to remember.

ideas.idea: LinkedIn is no longer just for active job seekers; it is your online front page and personal brand, and not having an optimized profile is a detriment.
ideas.detail: The hosts cite a New York Times piece asking whether LinkedIn is entering its 'post-cringe era'; keeping people updated on what you are doing lets organic opportunities arrive outside your direct job.

ideas.idea: Create the narrative you want about yourself before one is created for you; the point of LinkedIn is presenting yourself so more opportunities become available.
ideas.detail: Cherie calls the profile sections underused 'real estate' where you can talk about yourself in your own voice.

ideas.idea: Behind the scenes LinkedIn is all metadata, so the more sections you fill out (experience, skills, recommendations, volunteering) the more you surface in recruiter searches.
ideas.detail: Cherie worked on the profile team and says a recruiter filtering for someone in the Bay Area with ABC skills and certain experience will only find you if that data is registered on your profile. Goal: be discoverable.

ideas.idea: Write your About section with the 'three S's': share who you are, sell what you do and offer, and become search optimized in your audience's language.
ideas.detail: This is Cherie's own framework from her Stanford GSB lecture; search optimization means adding metadata via the About text so people actually find you.

ideas.idea: Most people, even Stanford MBAs with about five years of work experience, leave the About section empty; something is better than nothing, so start with one to three sentences.
ideas.detail: Hands-up polls in Cherie's Stanford class come out 50/50 or 70/30 with most not having it filled out. Beginners should not skip ahead to advanced tactics.

ideas.idea: Aim to be 'one in a million, not one of a million': a good About could only describe you.
ideas.detail: Borrowed from Cherie's writing professor Glenn Kramer. Example: a VP of product whose one sentence spans the first US hybrid SUV, a number one app, a children's book and 'some parts of this page' (he led the LinkedIn profile team).

ideas.idea: Include quantitative figures wherever possible in your About and resume; concrete numbers root your accomplishments.
ideas.detail: Examples praised: 'number one app', '20+ years in exec roles at companies of 1 to 25,000 employees', 'raised $10M+ of VC funding as a co-founder in my early 20s', even a 4.98 Uber rating.

ideas.idea: Senior people can afford smiley faces, emojis and heavy personal content; if you are junior and want to be taken seriously, lead with professional substance.
ideas.detail: A COO's About lists five things of which three are personal (BJJ brown belt, dancer, powerlifter), but his Harvard, Google and LinkedIn history supports it; the hosts say such people have 'earned the right' to be playful.

ideas.idea: If you are building an audience or a business, make your About heavy on the 'sell' with a clear call to action.
ideas.detail: A founder's About reads 'My goal is to teach you how to start your own business one day. Follow to get my lessons learned building a billion dollar company'; a slight stretch is fine as long as the rest of the profile supports it.

ideas.idea: An emoji-bulleted list of memorable, numeric, tongue-in-cheek facts is a strong intermediate format because it is easy to parse and impossible to confuse with anyone else.
ideas.detail: The example profile mixes 20+ years of exec roles and $10M raised with semi-pro basketball in Europe, top-three archery in Germany, travelling with his own tea and meditating with monks; Cherie's Stanford class splits 50/50 between 'cringe' and 'hilarious', but everyone remembers him.

ideas.idea: Short, constrained writing is harder and more valuable than long paragraphs, especially now that AI can generate paragraphs in a second.
ideas.detail: Many About sections are unreadable paragraphs; the hosts prefer a few specific sentences boiled down.

ideas.idea: Use emojis only where they make sense for the content that follows; random emojis are a tell of AI-generated text.
ideas.detail: An arrow for archery and a basketball for basketball reads as human; AI tends to throw in unrelated emojis.

ideas.idea: Put your mission statement at the very top of your profile so readers know what you care about and why, not just where you worked.
ideas.detail: Cherie's reads 'empower one billion people to advance in their careers and be the trusted voice women ages 13 to 35 turn to'; her professor calls it one of the best About sections he has seen. Ask yourself: what matters most to you and why?

ideas.idea: Structure your About as mission (share), call to action with contact (sell), then fun facts (one-in-a-million talking points).
ideas.detail: Cherie lists 'looking to collaborate: partnerships@tigersisters.co', then facts like living on a Japanese tea farm, co-founding Sisters Matcha, loving Hamilton, and being a LinkedIn Learning instructor; personal connection points beat purely professional ones.

ideas.idea: Generic openers like 'passionate about solving complex product challenges, collaborating and driving results' are bad because they could be anyone and sound AI-written.
ideas.detail: Cherie flags a friend's profile opener and 'I welcome conversations of any kind' as one-of-a-million filler to avoid.

ideas.idea: LinkedIn is a search engine, so naturally weave in the titles, skills, industries, tools and companies that genuinely apply to you rather than keyword-stuffing.
ideas.detail: An advanced example dumps a list of Google, Facebook, McKinsey, Goldman Sachs, YC, Harvard etc. labelled as 'testing SEO terms for Sales Navigator'; Cherie says recruiters' searches scrape every profile field, but only include terms applicable to you.

ideas.idea: Write your own About rather than using LinkedIn's built-in AI writer; what you write yourself is currently better, and AI is only a Hail Mary when you have no time.
ideas.detail: The hosts say listeners will do a better job after the episode's frameworks.

ideas.idea: Write the About in first person so your own voice shines through; third person feels removed, like a biography rather than an autobiography.
ideas.detail: Jean notes some people find first person boastful, but readers know it is about you and first person reads stronger.

ideas.idea: Test your About with one question: what is the one sentence you want people to remember after reading it? If you cannot answer easily, revise.
ideas.detail: The closing exercise; part two of the masterclass will review listener-submitted profiles.
